title: Startup Launchpad
theme: Build a startup from idea to funding in the Indian ecosystem
description: You've got a game-changing idea and the fire to build something big! Navigate the wild world of startups — from building your MVP to pitching investors, hiring your first team, and scaling up. Can you build the next Indian unicorn?
learning_objectives: Understand the startup lifecycle from ideation to scaling
Learn about MVP development and product-market fit
Practice pitching ideas and negotiating with investors
Understand team building and leadership fundamentals
Explore the Indian startup ecosystem and its opportunities

ai_image_config.art_direction: Modern startup culture illustration, Indian teens building technology, co-working spaces, pitch events, vibrant and inspiring, contemporary Indian urban tech scene

scenes.title: The Idea Spark
scenes.narrative: You're at a hackathon at IIT when it hits you — an app idea that could solve a real problem for millions of Indian students. You've been coding for fun, but this could be your shot at building something real. Your heart races as you start scribbling the concept on a napkin.
scenes.image_prompt: Excited Indian teenager at a hackathon event, surrounded by laptops and whiteboards with app wireframes, other young innovators in background, modern tech event lighting, vibrant startup culture illustration

choices.label: I'll build an AI-powered study app that creates personalised plans for board exam prep
choices.description: An AI-powered app that creates personalized study plans for board exams.

choices.label: I want to build a platform that rewards people with points for doing eco-friendly things like recycling
choices.description: An app that rewards users with points for sustainable actions like recycling.

choices.label: I think a hyper-local app connecting neighbourhood shops with teen customers could really work
choices.description: A hyper-local platform connecting neighborhood shops with teen customers.

scenes.title: Finding Your Co-Founder
scenes.narrative: Every great startup needs a great team. You can't do this alone. At the hackathon afterparty, you meet two potential co-founders: Deepa, a brilliant coder who's won 3 hackathons, and Aryan, a natural leader who's president of the Entrepreneurship Cell.
scenes.image_prompt: Three Indian teenagers having an animated conversation at a modern co-working cafe, laptops open with app designs, startup posters on walls, collaborative and energetic atmosphere, colorful illustration

choices.label: I'll team up with Deepa — her coding skills will help us build a solid product fast
choices.description: Deepa's coding skills will help build a solid product fast.

choices.label: I should partner with Aryan — his business connections and growth mindset will help us scale
choices.description: Aryan's connections and business sense will help with growth and funding.

choices.label: I'll convince both Deepa and Aryan to join — a bigger team means we can move faster together
choices.description: A bigger team means more equity split but faster execution.

scenes.title: Ready to Launch!
scenes.narrative: Your team is set, the idea is clear, and you've got seed money from a college startup grant of ₹1,00,000. But two other teams from the hackathon are building similar ideas — TechForward (well-funded) and GreenStart (scrappy but creative). The race is on!
scenes.image_prompt: Indian teenager team in a small startup office launching their app on a laptop, celebration moment with confetti, competitors visible through the window working on their own startups, dynamic and competitive illustration

npcs.name: Vikram Mehta
npcs.personality: Sharp, data-driven, asks tough questions. Impressed by traction and metrics, not just ideas. Friendly but expects professionalism.
npcs.backstory: Partner at a top Bangalore-based VC firm that has backed 12 unicorns. He started his career at IIM-A and believes India's next generation of entrepreneurs will come from tier-2 cities. He's mentored 50+ startups.
npcs.system_prompt_addon: You are an Indian VC partner. Ask about metrics (MRR, DAU, CAC, LTV). Reference Indian startups (Zerodha, CRED, PhonePe, Razorpay). Give tough but fair feedback on startup ideas. Explain VC concepts simply.

npcs.name: Deepa
npcs.personality: Practical, solution-oriented, sometimes perfectionist about code quality. Cares deeply about user experience.
npcs.backstory: A 16-year-old coding prodigy who taught herself Python at 12 and has built 5 apps. She's won hackathons at IIT and BITS. She believes great products are built with empathy for users, not just clever code.
npcs.system_prompt_addon: You are a teen tech co-founder in India. Talk about building MVPs, React Native, Firebase, AWS. Give practical development advice. Advocate for user-centric design. Mention Indian tech tools and platforms.

npcs.name: Prof. Iyer
npcs.personality: Experienced, philosophical, connects startup lessons to life principles. Uses stories from Indian business history.
npcs.backstory: A retired IIM professor who has mentored over 100 startups through government incubators. He believes entrepreneurship is not just about money — it's about solving problems and building character.
npcs.system_prompt_addon: You are a wise Indian business mentor. Reference Indian entrepreneurs (Narayana Murthy, Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw, Bhavish Aggarwal). Share startup wisdom through stories. Talk about government schemes (Startup India, MUDRA). Be philosophical but practical.

competitors.name: TechForward (Aditya's Team)
competitors.description: Well-funded team led by Aditya, whose parents are in tech. They have ₹2,00,000 in seed money and a polished pitch deck. They move fast and spend big on growth.
competitors.chat_personality: Confident, sometimes arrogant about their funding advantage. Competitive but can be rattled when the player outperforms them on metrics.

competitors.name: GreenStart (Meera's Team)
competitors.description: Bootstrapped team led by Meera, passionate about sustainability. Less money but incredible product quality and a loyal early user base.
competitors.chat_personality: Humble, focused on impact over money. Respects good product decisions. Competitive through quality, not spending.

base_rounds.title: Round 1: Building the MVP
base_rounds.story: Your idea is great but you need to build a Minimum Viable Product fast. You have 4 weeks before the college demo day. Deepa says she can build a basic version, but you need to decide what features make the cut. Remember: 'If you're not embarrassed by v1, you launched too late!'
base_rounds.image_prompt: Indian teenagers coding intensely on laptops in a college dorm room late at night, sticky notes and wireframe sketches covering the wall, empty chai cups on the desk, warm lamp light, vibrant startup culture illustration
base_rounds.goal: Build your MVP by choosing the right features and approach

choices.label: Lean MVP (Core Features Only)
choices.description: Build just the essential feature. Launch in 2 weeks, iterate based on feedback.
choices.feedback: The lean startup approach! Reid Hoffman said 'If you're not embarrassed by v1, you launched too late.' Your stripped-down MVP gets to users fast. Early feedback is more valuable than perfect code. This is how WhatsApp and Instagram started!

choices.label: Feature-Rich MVP
choices.description: Build a complete v1 with multiple features. Takes all 4 weeks but looks polished.
choices.feedback: An ambitious build! Your product looks impressive, but it took the full 4 weeks and drained team energy. The risk with feature-rich MVPs is spending too long building features users might not want. But the polish could wow demo day judges!

choices.label: No-Code Quick Launch
choices.description: Use Bubble/Glide to build a prototype in 1 week. Fast but limited functionality.
choices.feedback: Speed to market wins! No-code tools let you test your idea before investing in development. Many Indian startups (including early Meesho) started with basic tools before building custom tech. You can always rebuild later with real code!

base_rounds.timeout_feedback: Time ran out! Indecision has consequences — you lost ground on key metrics.

base_rounds.title: Round 2: Getting First Users
base_rounds.story: Your MVP is live! But an app with zero users is just code sitting on a server. You need to get your first 100 users. TechForward is running Facebook ads. GreenStart is going door-to-door. What's your growth strategy?
base_rounds.image_prompt: Indian teenager enthusiastically demonstrating a mobile app to a crowd of curious students in a bustling college campus courtyard, smartphones in hands, download notifications floating upward, energetic and colorful illustration
base_rounds.goal: Acquire your first 100 users and validate product-market fit

choices.label: Launch in Your School First
choices.description: Make your school the testing ground. Get 100 users from students you know personally.
choices.feedback: The 'start small, dominate local' strategy! Facebook started at Harvard before expanding. By launching in your school, you get passionate early adopters who'll give honest feedback. Many Indian startups started hyperlocal — Zomato started with just restaurants near IIT Delhi!

choices.label: Social Media Viral Push
choices.description: Create viral content (memes, challenges) to drive organic downloads.
choices.feedback: Going viral is the startup dream! Your creative content attracts a wave of downloads. But viral users are fickle — many will delete the app after the hype dies. The key is converting them to daily active users (DAU). CRED's viral ads brought millions but retention was the real challenge!

choices.label: Partner with a School Network
choices.description: Convince a chain of coaching centers to pilot your app with their students.
choices.feedback: B2B partnerships are powerful! By partnering with an institution, you get a built-in user base and credibility. BYJU'S early growth came from partnerships with schools. The slower start is offset by higher quality, committed users!

base_rounds.title: Round 3: The Big Pitch
base_rounds.story: A prestigious startup accelerator (like Y Combinator India) is hosting Demo Day. You have 5 minutes to pitch your startup to a panel of VCs including Vikram Mehta. TechForward has a slick 50-slide deck. GreenStart is showing raw user testimonials. How do you pitch?
base_rounds.image_prompt: Indian teenager confidently presenting on stage at a startup demo day event, large screen showing growth charts behind them, panel of venture capitalists listening intently in the audience, dramatic stage lighting, cinematic illustration
base_rounds.goal: Deliver a compelling pitch to win investor interest

choices.label: Tell a Story
choices.description: Start with a personal story about why this problem matters. Emotional and memorable.
choices.feedback: Stories sell! Steve Jobs didn't pitch specs — he told stories about changing the world. Your personal connection to the problem made VCs lean in. Vikram Mehta said: 'I invest in people, not slide decks.' A great story shows passion and conviction!

choices.label: Data-Driven Pitch
choices.description: Lead with metrics: user numbers, retention rates, market size. Let the data speak.
choices.feedback: Numbers don't lie! VCs love founders who know their metrics. Your TAM/SAM/SOM analysis showed market potential, and your retention data proved product-market fit. Vikram Mehta was impressed: 'This founder knows their unit economics.'

choices.label: Live Product Demo
choices.description: Skip the slides. Show the product working in real-time. Risky but impressive.
choices.feedback: Bold move! A live demo shows confidence in your product. When it works, nothing is more convincing. But live demos can also go wrong (the infamous 'demo effect'). Your smooth execution showed VCs that your product is real, not vaporware!

base_rounds.timeout_feedback: Time ran out! Indecision has consequences — you lost ground on key metrics.

base_rounds.title: Round 4: Growing the Team
base_rounds.story: Your startup is gaining traction and you need to hire. But talent is expensive and making bad hires can sink a startup faster than running out of money. You have budget for 2 new hires. What roles do you prioritize?
base_rounds.image_prompt: Indian startup founder interviewing candidates in a modern co-working space, resumes and portfolios spread on a glass table, diverse young professionals waiting in the background, bright collaborative atmosphere, vibrant illustration
base_rounds.goal: Make smart hiring decisions to strengthen your team

choices.label: 2 Engineers
choices.description: Double your development speed. Ship features faster and fix bugs quicker.
choices.feedback: Engineering power! More developers means faster iteration cycles. But remember — adding engineers to a project can sometimes slow things down initially (Brooks' Law: 'Adding people to a late project makes it later'). After the ramp-up, your product velocity will soar!

choices.label: 1 Engineer + 1 Marketer
choices.description: Balance product development with growth. Build and sell simultaneously.
choices.feedback: The balanced approach! Having both builders and sellers is crucial for startups. Your engineer improves the product while your marketer drives growth. This is the ideal early-stage composition — many successful startups have a technical + business founding combo!

choices.label: 4 Interns Instead
choices.description: Hire enthusiastic college interns at lower cost. More hands, smaller impact per person.
choices.feedback: Budget-friendly! Interns bring energy and fresh ideas. Many Indian startups like Flipkart relied heavily on interns in early days. The trade-off is less experience and more management overhead. But you saved significant funding for other needs!

base_rounds.title: Round 5: Scale or Die
base_rounds.story: Your app has 5,000 users and growing. But TechForward just raised ₹50 lakh and is scaling aggressively. GreenStart was featured in YourStory and users are flooding in. The market is heating up — if you don't scale now, you'll be left behind. Prof. Iyer says: 'Growth without profit is just expensive exercise.'
base_rounds.image_prompt: Aerial view of an Indian startup war room with multiple screens showing user growth dashboards and competitor analytics, young team members strategizing around a large table, city skyline through floor-to-ceiling windows, intense and dramatic lighting

choices.label: Blitzscale!
choices.description: Raise more funding, burn cash on growth. Speed over efficiency.
choices.feedback: Blitzscaling — the strategy made famous by LinkedIn's Reid Hoffman! You prioritize speed over efficiency, growing fast to capture the market. Ola and Jio used this approach. The risk? High burn rate and you're dependent on continuous funding.

choices.label: Sustainable Growth
choices.description: Grow organically. Focus on unit economics and become profitable.
choices.feedback: The Zerodha way! Nithin Kamath built Zerodha to profitability without raising VC money. Sustainable growth means you control your destiny. Slower than blitzscaling, but you're building a real business, not a house of cards. India's most enduring companies grew steadily!

choices.label: Strategic Pivot
choices.description: Based on user data, pivot to a more profitable market segment.
choices.feedback: The brave choice! Slack started as a gaming company before pivoting to messaging. Instagram started as Burbn (a location app) before pivoting to photos. Sometimes the best growth strategy is finding a better market. Your data-driven pivot shows maturity!

base_rounds.timeout_feedback: Time ran out! Indecision has consequences — you lost ground on key metrics.

how_to_play: Start with the story intro — your idea and team choices shape your startup's DNA
Each round presents a real startup challenge to navigate
Chat with Vikram Mehta for investor perspective, Deepa for tech advice, or Prof. Iyer for business wisdom
Watch TechForward and GreenStart — they'll react to your moves and compete for market share
Balance funding, product quality, team morale, and user growth
AI generates unique startup challenges based on your strategy
Build the most successful startup by the end of the game

crisis_events.title: User Feedback Crisis!
crisis_events.description: Your first users have left harsh feedback about the MVP, citing major flaws and bugs. Failure to address this could lead to a loss in reputation and user base.

choices.label: Fix the Bugs
choices.description: Allocate resources to fix bugs and improve product quality.
choices.feedback: You improved the product, but the cost affected your reputation as you diverted funds.

choices.label: Ignore the Feedback
choices.description: Continue with your current plan and focus on user acquisition.
choices.feedback: Your user base grew, but the negative feedback damaged your reputation significantly.

crisis_events.title: Team Conflict!
crisis_events.description: A disagreement between team members has escalated, threatening morale and productivity. You need to act fast to prevent a breakdown.

choices.label: Mediate the Conflict
choices.description: Take time to resolve the conflict through team discussions.
choices.feedback: The mediation improved morale, but you had to use some funding for team activities.

choices.label: Dismiss a Team Member
choices.description: Remove the source of conflict from the team.
choices.feedback: This drastic action increased tension within the team, impacting morale and your reputation.

crisis_events.title: Investor Rejection!
crisis_events.description: After a tense pitch, key investors have rejected your startup due to concerns over product viability. This could hinder your growth potential.

choices.label: Rework the Pitch
choices.description: Spend time perfecting your pitch and addressing feedback for the next opportunity.
choices.feedback: The reworked pitch improved your reputation, but it cost you valuable funding and delayed your plans.

choices.label: Seek Alternative Investors
choices.description: Quickly pivot to other, less experienced investors to secure immediate funding.
choices.feedback: You secured funds quickly, but the less credible investors hurt your overall reputation.

interdependencies.message: When product quality is low, it leads to negative user experiences, causing a significant drop in the user base as potential customers are discouraged from trying the product.
Low team morale can lead to a lack of enthusiasm and poor performance, which negatively impacts the company's reputation as customers perceive a lack of commitment and quality.
High funding allows for better resources and tools to enhance product quality, leading to more innovative features and a superior user experience, thus improving the overall product.

endings.title: Legendary Success
endings.description: Congratulations! You've transformed your innovative idea into a thriving startup, garnering immense user engagement and recognition. Your journey inspires countless young entrepreneurs across India, proving that with passion and perseverance, anything is possible.

endings.title: Good Ending
endings.description: Well done! Your startup has made significant strides, attracting a dedicated user base and positive feedback. You've learned valuable lessons about teamwork and innovation, setting a strong foundation for future success.

endings.title: Okay Ending
endings.description: You've made it through the startup journey with some achievements under your belt. While there were challenges, your experiences have equipped you with the knowledge and skills to tackle future endeavors with more confidence.

endings.title: Learning Journey
endings.description: Every entrepreneur faces ups and downs. Though the journey may not have ended as you hoped, you've gained essential insights into the world of startups. Remember, every setback is a setup for a comeback!

glossary_terms.definition: Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement — your fallback if no deal is reached.
glossary_terms.example: If you can't agree on a price, you could sell to a different buyer — that's your BATNA.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: A strong BATNA gives negotiating power. Knowing both parties' BATNAs reveals who needs the deal more.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: A job applicant with another offer has a stronger BATNA and can negotiate more confidently.

glossary_terms.definition: Finding solutions where both parties gain value rather than one side winning at the other's expense.
glossary_terms.example: Agreeing on a payment plan that works for both buyer and seller, rather than a discount that hurts profit.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Integrative negotiation expands the 'pie' by identifying trade-offs where each party values things differently.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Labor-management negotiations that increase productivity in exchange for better wages can benefit both sides.

glossary_terms.definition: Setting an initial reference point in a negotiation that influences the final outcome.
glossary_terms.example: The first price mentioned in a negotiation becomes the anchor around which all counteroffers are compared.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Research shows people are heavily influenced by the first number they hear, even when irrelevant.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Salary negotiations: starting with a high number tends to result in higher final offers.
